lead: Gears transmit rotation and torque between shafts at a fixed ratio. The law of gearing says the common normal at every contact point must pass through the pitch point. The involute profile meets this condition, so the ratio stays constant even when the centre distance changes slightly. You see gears in a UPI payment machine's paper drive, in a two-wheeler gearbox and in a Chennai pump set. This chapter names the parts of a tooth and shows why the involute is the standard shape.
prereq: You need: school geometry of circles and triangles, and the relation v = πdn/60 from Unit 6, Design of flat belt drives.

blocks.text: Gears are chosen first by how their shafts sit. Spur gears have straight teeth and parallel shafts. They are simple and efficient, but the whole tooth engages at once, so they are noisy at high speed. Helical gears also have parallel shafts, but the teeth are cut at a helix angle. Contact starts at one end and slides along the tooth, so the drive is quieter and carries more load; the price is an axial thrust that the bearings must take. Bevel gears sit on cones and connect intersecting shafts, usually at 90°. A worm and worm wheel connect crossed shafts, usually at right angles, and give a large reduction in one step through sliding contact. A rack is a gear with infinite pitch radius: it turns rotation into straight-line motion, as in a car steering rack or a sliding door opener. An internal gear has teeth cut on the inside of a ring, so the pinion sits inside it and the pair is compact.

Every gear calculation starts at the pitch circle. It is the imaginary circle on which the teeth roll without slipping. Let d be the pitch circle diameter in mm and z the number of teeth. The module is m = d/z, in mm. Module is the standard index of tooth size: a 4 mm module means 4 mm of pitch diameter for every tooth. The circular pitch is the distance from one tooth to the next measured along the pitch circle: p = πd/z = πm, in mm. A 4 mm module therefore has p = 12.57 mm. In inch units, diametral pitch P = z/d with d in inches; P is teeth per inch of pitch diameter, and m = 25.4/P. Some syllabi call m the metric module and P the English module.

Tooth height follows the module. Standard full-depth teeth use addendum h_a = m above the pitch circle and dedendum h_f = 1.25m below it. Clearance is c = 0.25m, working depth is 2m and whole depth is 2.25m. The pressure angle φ is the angle between the common normal at the pitch point and the common tangent; 20° is the standard. The base circle diameter is d_b = d cos φ, because the involute is generated from this smaller circle. Face width b is the tooth length along the shaft. For two external gears the centre distance is a = m(z1+z2)/2; for an internal pair use a = m(z2−z1)/2 with z2 the internal gear.

sections.h3: The law of gearing and the involute

blocks.text: The law of gearing fixes the shape of a tooth. At any instant a pair of teeth touches at a point. Draw the common normal to the two profiles at that point. The law says this normal must cut the line joining the two shaft centres at a fixed point, the pitch point, for the speed ratio to stay constant. If the normal wanders, the ratio changes tooth by tooth, and the drive vibrates. Notice that it is the common normal, not the common tangent.

The involute curve satisfies the law. Imagine a taut string unwinding from a base circle; the end traces an involute. At every contact point the common normal is the string itself, tangent to both base circles, and it always passes through the pitch point. The velocity ratio is therefore constant: ω1/ω2 = d2/d1 = z2/z1, where ω is angular speed in rad/s. A small change in centre distance does not change this ratio for an involute pair, because the base circles do not change; only the pressure angle shifts. That tolerance to mounting error is why involute gears dominate.

Interference occurs when contact tries to happen on the non-involute part of a tooth, below the base circle. A small pinion with a large gear is the usual case. The cutter then removes material from the pinion root, called undercutting, and the tooth becomes weak. Minimum tooth numbers and profile shift are the standard cures; tooth stress itself is covered in Chapter 7.3.

examples.question: A 20° involute spur pair has z1 = 20, z2 = 60 and module 4 mm. Find both pitch diameters, the centre distance, both base circle diameters and the velocity ratio.
steps: Module is m = d/z, so d1 = m z1 = 4 × 20 = 80 mm and d2 = m z2 = 4 × 60 = 240 mm.
External centre distance is a = (d1 + d2)/2 = (80 + 240)/2 = 160 mm.
Base circle diameter is d_b = d cos φ. With φ = 20°, cos 20° = 0.93969. Then d_b1 = 80 × 0.93969 = 75.175 mm ≈ 75.2 mm and d_b2 = 240 × 0.93969 = 225.526 mm ≈ 225.5 mm.
Velocity ratio is ω1/ω2 = z2/z1 = 60/20 = 3. The pinion turns three times for one turn of the gear.
examples.answer: The pitch diameters are 80 mm and 240 mm, the centre distance is 160 mm, the base circle diameters are 75.2 mm and 225.5 mm, and the velocity ratio is 3.
examples.check:
import math
m = 4
z1 = 20
z2 = 60
phi = math.radians(20)
d1 = m * z1
d2 = m * z2
a = (d1 + d2) / 2
db1 = d1 * math.cos(phi)
db2 = d2 * math.cos(phi)
ratio = z2 / z1
print(f"{d1:.1f}")
print(f"{d2:.1f}")
print(f"{a:.1f}")
print(f"{db1:.1f}")
print(f"{db2:.1f}")
print(f"{ratio:.1f}")

traps: Module uses the pitch circle: m = d/z. Using the addendum circle or the base circle gives a wrong module.
Circular pitch is p = πm, not m. Module is not the tooth thickness or the pitch.
The law of gearing is about the common normal at the contact point, not the common tangent. Examiners test this wording.
Diametral pitch is in inch units: P = z/d with d in inches, and m = 25.4/P. Mixing mm with P gives a wrong module.
For an internal gear pair the centre distance is m(z2 − z1)/2. Adding the tooth numbers is wrong.

quiz.q: Define module and give its unit.
quiz.a: Module m = d/z, where d is the pitch circle diameter in mm and z is the number of teeth. Its unit is mm.

quiz.q: Why does an involute profile satisfy the law of gearing?
quiz.a: The common normal at every contact point is tangent to both base circles and passes through the fixed pitch point. So the common normal divides the line of centres in a constant ratio, giving a constant velocity ratio.

quiz.q: A 20° involute spur pair has z1 = 18, z2 = 54 and module 3 mm. Find d1, d2, the centre distance and the pinion base circle diameter.
In an involute pair the centre distance is increased by 0.5 mm. What happens to the velocity ratio and the pressure angle?
quiz.a: The velocity ratio stays z2/z1 because the base circles and tooth numbers do not change. The pressure angle increases slightly, and the contact ratio changes. The teeth still conjugate.

quiz.q: Name the gear type used for intersecting shafts, usually at 90°.
Why are helical gears quieter than spur gears, and what extra load do they create?
quiz.a: Helical teeth contact gradually along the face width instead of all at once, so impact and noise are lower. The helix creates an axial thrust that the bearings and shaft must carry.

quiz.q: Find the circular pitch of a gear with module 5 mm.
Why does undercutting happen in a small pinion meshing with a large gear?
quiz.a: The contact tries to extend below the base circle, where the involute does not exist. The cutter removes material from the pinion root to avoid interference. This weakens the tooth; minimum tooth numbers or profile shift avoid it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern gearboxes use profile-modified and asymmetric involute teeth to reduce noise and raise load capacity. Powder-metal and plastic gears are common in small appliances, while ground and case-hardened gears dominate automotive and wind-turbine drives. Research focuses on micro-geometry, transmission error and surface tribology. Search next: profile shift, tip relief, lead crowning, gear metrology.
